issues.title: Use keyword-only and position arg-only function signatures where reasonable
issues.body:
We could eliminate some of the confusion we've had with position parameters having sufficiently common names that they get overloaded with keywords.  This was the reason for changing the name of position arguments in the graph constructors for example.  So, it seems that the position-only "/" (PEP 570) and keyword-only "*" (PEP 3102) syntax changes might be helpful in some places.
```python
def to_undirected(*, reciprocal=False, as_view=False):
```
would avoid the trouble pointed out in #3994 

Let's move toward that signature where it is helpful to do so.

Unfortunately, position-only parameter syntax: "/" is not available until python 3.8 and I don't see any way to get 3.7 to use it.
Does anyone know a way to get "/" to work in python 3.7?
issues.author: dschult

comments.body:
I just stumbled across discussions in other projects on whether/how to adopt keyword-only arguments, e.g. scipy/scipy#14714. It appears scikit-learn has adopted this already and has a well-thought-out policy: https://scikit-learn-enhancement-proposals.readthedocs.io/en/latest/slep009/proposal.html

FWIW there is a general consensus that keyword-only arguments are a great idea for *new* functions.
comments.author: rossbar

comments.body:
> Unfortunately, position-only parameter syntax: "/" is not available until python 3.8 and I don't see any way to get 3.7 to use it.
> Does anyone know a way to get "/" to work in python 3.7?

Now that you've long dropped 3.7, it may be worth revisiting this?
comments.author: NeilGirdhar

comments.body: @NeilGirdhar thanks for bumping this up, we have already started using keyword only args in new functions were it makes sense. For the LSP violation in DiGraph https://github.com/networkx/networkx/issues/3994 we need to either come up with a backward compatible hack or  go through a proper deprecation cycle to warn users.
comments.author: MridulS

comments.body:
> through a proper deprecation cycle to warn users.

Good idea.  Probably the sooner the better?
comments.author: NeilGirdhar

comments.body: I recall thinking about this while writing the `argmap` meta-decorator, and it was regarded as complexity we didn't need.  I've been away from networkx for a few months, but if somebody hits a snag there, please @mention me or email me!
comments.author: boothby

comments.body:
This remains a good idea, but is a large enough change that it (IMO) requires an NXEP. I think the best way forward would be to follow the scikit-learn model: https://scikit-learn-enhancement-proposals.readthedocs.io/en/latest/slep009/proposal.html

I was fortunate enough to chat with @glemaitre at the scientific Python summit about sklearn's experience implementing SLEP009. In general, it seems the experience was positive and there was not a lot of push-back from users.

Here's what a compelling proposal would look like (to me):
 1. Draft an NXEP using SLEP009 as a reference
 2. Compile a listing of the NX public API and document where we'd propose to add the kwarg-only star in each case.

Once consensus has been reached in these steps, adopt the decorator used by sklearn to implement the deprecation warning, and leave the deprecations in place for 2 cycles. It may also be worthwhile to increment the major version (i.e. release NetworkX 4.0) when the deprecation expires.
comments.author: rossbar

comments.body: FWIW: Matplolib has also been gradually moving towards kw-only arguments over the past couple of years, and experience is positive. We haven't had any complains from the user side, and the positive aspects of stricter signatures have started to pay off in making it easier to adapt signatures, be it that we can reasonably group related kw arguments or in some cases also redesign the API.
comments.author: timhoffm

issues.title: capacity_scaling returns a zero-cost infeasible flow instead of raising NetworkXUnfeasible
issues.body:
networkx 3.7 and main (92f497e).

```python
import networkx as nx
G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_node(0, demand=1)
G.add_node(1, demand=-1)
G.add_edge(1, 0, capacity=0, weight=1)

nx.network_simplex(G)   # raises NetworkXUnfeasible (correct)
nx.min_cost_flow(G)     # raises NetworkXUnfeasible (correct)
nx.capacity_scaling(G)  # returns (0, {0: {}, 1: {0: 0}}), no exception
```

The returned flow does not meet the demands (net flow 0 at both nodes vs demands 1 and -1). The graph is weakly connected and the demands sum to zero. The docstring says NetworkXUnfeasible is raised when "There is no flow satisfying all demand" (capacityscaling.py:228). A graph with the same two demands and no edges at all behaves the same way.

Cause: the "Residual network has no edges" early return (capacityscaling.py:297-300) fires before the excess check at capacityscaling.py:396-397, so the infeasibility is never detected.

(Found with the help of an AI code-auditing agent; I reran the reproducer above on 3.7.)
issues.author: Aspect5

issues.title: `minimum_spanning_arborescence` / `maximum_spanning_arborescence` raise "No ... spanning arborescence in G" on graphs that have one (regression since 3.2)
issues.body:
### Current Behavior

On some graphs that do have a spanning arborescence,
`nx.minimum_spanning_arborescence` raises
`NetworkXException: No minimum spanning arborescence in G.`
`nx.maximum_spanning_arborescence` does the same on the negated weights.

### Expected Behavior

Return the minimum (maximum) spanning arborescence. In the example below it
is unique: `3→1, 1→4, 4→0, 0→2`, weight 31.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import networkx as nx

E = [(0, 1, 1.0), (0, 2, 10.0), (0, 4, 1.0), (1, 4, 10.0),
     (2, 4, 0.4), (3, 1, 10.0), (4, 0, 1.0)]
G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_weighted_edges_from(E)

# a spanning arborescence exists (vertex 3 is the only vertex without in-edges):
T = nx.DiGraph([(3, 1), (1, 4), (4, 0), (0, 2)])
assert nx.is_arborescence(T) and all(G.has_edge(*e) for e in T.edges)

nx.minimum_spanning_arborescence(G)   # raises NetworkXException

H = nx.DiGraph()
H.add_weighted_edges_from((u, v, -w) for u, v, w in E)
nx.maximum_spanning_arborescence(H)   # raises too
```

Results by version:

| networkx | result |
| --- | --- |
| 2.8.8, 3.0, 3.1 | returns `[(0, 2), (1, 4), (3, 1), (4, 0)]`, weight 31 |
| 3.2, 3.2.1, 3.3, 3.4.2, 3.5, 3.6.1, 3.7, `main` (6da4704) | raises |

### Cause

Since 3.2, `minimum_spanning_arborescence` calls `minimal_branching`. That
function re-weights each edge to `w' = C - w` with
`C = 2*max_weight - min_weight + 1`, takes a maximum branching, and relies
on that branching being spanning.

A branching with k trees has n - k edges. So maximizing `sum(w')` is the
same as minimizing `w(B) + C*k`: every extra tree costs C. That only forces
a spanning result when C exceeds the largest possible saving in `w` from
dropping to fewer edges, and that saving can be about n times the weight
spread. Here, n = 5, max = 10, min = 0, so C = 21.

- The only spanning arborescence has w = 31, so with the fee:
  31 + 21 = **52**.
- The 2-tree branching `0→1, 2→4, 4→0` has w = 2.4, so with the fees:
  2.4 + 2*21 = **44.4**.

The branching wins, and the `is_arborescence` check raises. Merging its
two trees needs a swap: drop 2 edges and add 3, i.e. +28.6 in w. That is
more than one C.

`maximum_spanning_arborescence` uses the analogous shift and fails the same
way. When the functions *do* return, the result is optimal. The bug only
produces false "no arborescence" exceptions, never a wrong tree.

### Possible fix

Any `C > (n - 1)*max_weight - (n - 2)*min_weight` makes every spanning
branching beat every non-spanning one. For example, use
`C = 2*sum(abs(w)) + 1`, or add the shift only as a per-root cost via a
virtual root. Alternatively, restore the pre-3.2 behavior: Edmonds'
arborescence mode, where every vertex with an in-edge takes its best
in-edge regardless of sign.

### How often

In a random search over small digraphs (3–7 vertices, mixed weights from
{0, 1, 10, U(0,1)}):

- networkx 3.6.1 raised on **54 of 169,169** graphs that have a spanning
  arborescence;
- networkx 3.1 raised on **0 of 168,890**.

### Environment

Python 3.11 / 3.13, Linux; networkx versions as in the table.
issues.author: shilo-a7x

issues.title: TSP methods has different functional prescription and function traveling_salesman_problem doesn't count with that
issues.body:
<!-- If you have a general question about NetworkX, please use the discussions tab to create a new discussion -->

<!--- Provide a general summary of the issue in the Title above -->


### Current Behavior
<!--- Tell us what happens instead of the expected behavior -->
The function [traveling_salesman_problem](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L199) choose TSP method by one of function parameters called "method". The problem is, that [christofides](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L127) and [greedy_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1094) has parameters G, weights="weights",... but [simulated_annealing_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1186) and [threshold_accepting_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1404) has parameters G, init_cycle, weights=weights, ... 
Function [traveling_salesman_problem](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L199) call this methods like this [method call](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L319):
```python
best_GG = method(GG, weight)
```
So methods [christofides](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L127) and [greedy_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1094) works well, but [simulated_annealing_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1186) and [threshold_accepting_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1404) ends with error because weights is put to init_cycle. 


### Expected Behavior
<!--- Tell us what should happen -->
Methods should have same functional prescription or function [traveling_salesman_problem](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L199) should has switch for methods.



### Steps to Reproduce
<!--- Provide a minimal example that reproduces the bug -->
```python
nodes_count = 10
edges = [(u,v) for u in range(nodes_count) for v in range(u+1,nodes_count)]
G = nx.Graph()
G.add_edges_from(edges)

nodes_tsp = [x for x in range(0,nodes_count,3)]
nx.algorithms.approximation.traveling_salesman_problem(G, nodes=nodes_tsp, method=nx.algorithms.approximation.christofides) # works
nx.algorithms.approximation.traveling_salesman_problem(G, nodes=nodes_tsp, method=nx.algorithms.approximation.greedy_tsp) # works
nx.algorithms.approximation.traveling_salesman_problem(G, nodes=nodes_tsp, method=nx.algorithms.approximation.threshold_accepting_tsp) # does not work
nx.algorithms.approximation.traveling_salesman_problem(G, nodes=nodes_tsp, method=nx.algorithms.approximation.simulated_annealing_tsp) # does not work
```

### Environment
<!--- Please provide details about your local environment -->
Python version: 3.7
NetworkX version: 2.7.1 (but actual version in github will have the same probelm)
issues.author: zabojpetr

comments.body:
Thanks very much for this!  

This is an intentional, yet confusing interface and probably should be improved. There are many ways in which this could be addressed. We currently rely on people using the `method` argument by constructing a function with 2 arguments. And our current doc_string lists these two problematic [simulated_annealing_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1186) and [threshold_accepting_tsp](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/7e17ff9007d2e71c2ea2a6d340889c331689343c/networkx/algorithms/approximation/traveling_salesman.py#L1404) functions as valid methods. And they are not currently valid. We even have code for the default method which wraps `threshold_accepting_tsp` so that it takes the required 2 arguments.  So we need to find a fix for this confusion. 

As a workaround while we find a fix, one can use:
`method = lambda G, weight: nx.algorithms.approximation.threshold_accepting_tsp(G, "greedy", weight)` and 
`method = lambda G, weight: nx.algorithms.approximation.simulated_annealing_tsp(G, "greedy", weight)`.  Note that this is the way we current allow people to provide other optional input to the TSP methods. Perhaps better documentation of that process -- including examples, would be helpful too.
comments.author: dschult

comments.body:
I thing that there are two main approaches we could take. Either we embrace the lambda expressions as the recommended way to do this, or we could use `**kwarg` or possibly have `traveling_salesman_problem` take in an extra dict which can be passed to which ever method is identified by the `method` keyword. Either way this should be totally optional. Since the definition of the traveling salesman problem only cares about the graph and the edge weights the other parameters like `init_cycle` for `threshold_accepting_tsp` should have a default since these tweak the behavior of the method but do not effect what we are seeking; an approximation of the minimum weight Hamiltonian cycle within a reasonable about of time.

Interestingly, the `init_cycle` that I mentioned says "This argument has no default to make you think about it" directly in the doc string, which does seem a bit odd to me.
comments.author: mjschwenne

comments.body:
I think we talked about `init_cycle` last summer too.  It is not clear what the default should be. The option "greedy" seems good at first, but it does take more time than we'd like. An arbitrary list of nodes like `list(G)` might be faster for some cases, but I don't have even experience to know.  I agree that the idea of not providing a default "to make you think about it" is a little strange -- though it is blunt enough to get the message across. It'd just be better if we knew what a good default was.

I think if we found a good default for `init_cycle` we could make the first two arguments to all the tsp methods be `G, weight` and it would simplify the interface. Then putting an example or two in the doc_string where we us a lambda function to supply non-default behavior would be sufficient.

Could we try a couple different `init_cycle` methods on some test graphs to see what tends to work best?
comments.author: dschult

comments.body:
Right, testing on some test graphs would probably be the best. It seems like the two methods to consider are 
 
 1. `greedy_tsp`
 2. `list(G) + [next(iter(G))]`
 
These cannot be replaced by say a boolean since, as the doc string mentions, it is possible that we want to use the output of another tsp method as input for the threshold accepting method. 

If some test graphs need to be designed, the principle concern is how large of graphs should we use to explore this problem? It looks like the greedy method is $O(n^2)$ and the other one is linear (I'd assume), so our question is then at what size does the cost of computing the greedy solution become not worth it. I suppose that another, preceding question would be does the greedy tsp solution yield a better approximation when used as the input for `threshold_accepting_tsp`? The number of edges doesn't matter since the tsp problem formulation dictates a complete graph and nothing else which would drastically affect performance comes to mind. 

This is one of those cases where knowing the size of graphs people are interested and capable of using these algorithms in becomes important. I'd guess 10  - 25 vertices, but I have nothing to go on other than my instinct. 

I may try to play with this question in the coming weeks, but my summer job starts tomorrow so we'll have to see how that goes.
comments.author: mjschwenne
